June 15, 2026  
 
 
 
VIA Regulations.gov  
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz, M.D., MBA 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS–0062–P 
Mail Stop C4–26–05 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244–1850 
 
Re: 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization – Request for Information for 
Laboratory Tests (CMS-0062-P) 
Dear Administrator Dr. Oz: 
Biodesix, Inc. writes to offer comment on CMS’s Request for Information (RFI) on prior 
authorization for laboratory tests.  We strongly support the agency’s commitment to addressing 
prior authorization practices used by Medicare Advantage Organizations (MAOs), which undercut 
access to clinical laboratory tests covered under National Coverage Determinations (NCDs) and 
Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs).   
Below we offer responses to the RFI.  We are particularly concerned about MAOs’ practices of 
failing to appropriately consider information on the laboratory test requisition form (TRF) in 
determining whether coverage criteria are met.  We agree with CMS that misuse of the original 
Medicare laboratory date of service (DOS) policy at 42 CFR § 414.510 and barring laboratories 
from obtaining prior authorization for their own tests are likewise highly problematic practices. 
The most straightforward way for CMS to address these issues with MAOs’ misuse of prior 
authorization to undermine their obligation to cover NCD- and LCD-covered tests is to prohibit 
the use of prior authorization by MAOs for a test covered by an NCD or LCD.  We likewise 
recommend that CMS clarify that it is impermissible for an MAO to impose a broad and 
burdensome policy of prepayment review for an NCD- or LCD-covered test.  At minimum, we 
urge the agency to make clear, in the Final Rule, that MAOs have the responsibility to process 
prior authorizations and claims for Medicare-covered services in an expeditious fashion, and we 
encourage CMS to provide an accessible enforcement pathway to report and correct misuse of 
prior authorization.   
I. 
Background 
Biodesix is an enrolled Medicare provider providing lung cancer diagnostic tests to address 
patient care from early diagnosis of lung nodules through late-stage cancer.  We submit claims to 
 
 
our Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs), Novitas Solutions and WPS GHA.  Our 
Nodify XL2, Nodify CDT, and VeriStrat clinical laboratory tests are covered by Medicare with 
established coverage criteria.  Below is the relevant clinical background on the tests and their 
Medicare coverage criteria. 
• Nodify XL2: Biodesix is the sole provider of the Nodify XL2 assay (CPT 0080U).1  The 
Nodify XL2 test is an analysis of two protein biomarkers combined using a proprietary 
algorithm with five clinical factors to assess the risk that identified pulmonary nodules 
are malignant.  The test serves a “rule-out” function, identifying patients with pulmonary 
nodules that are likely to be benign, thereby allowing physicians and patients to consider 
non-invasive measures like surveillance using computed tomography (CT) scanning. 
o All Nodify XL2 testing is performed at Biodesix’s De Soto, Kansas laboratory. 
Nodify XL2 is covered by the MAC for Kansas, WPS GHA, under LCD 
L37216.2  Nodify XL2 was approved as an Advanced Diagnostic Laboratory Test 
(ADLT) on May 17, 2019.   
 
• Nodify CDT: Biodesix is also the sole provider of the Nodify CDT test (0360U).3  
Nodify CDT is a “rule-in” test intended for use in patients with a pulmonary nodule who 
have been assessed to have a less than 65% risk of malignancy and who fall in the middle 
range of established clinical guidelines.  The test provides clinically relevant insight for 
both patient and physician in assessing whether there is a medical need for more timely 
intervention based on an algorithmic determination and reclassified risk of malignancy. 
Nodify CDT is a proteomic Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) test 
that analyzes the levels of seven autoantibodies (p53, NY-ESO-1, CAGE, GBU4-5, 
SOX2, MAGE A4, and HuD) to tumor-associated antigens.  These autoantibodies are 
measured utilizing ELISA and then combined with five clinical factors (age, smoking 
status, nodule diameter, edge characteristics, and nodule location) using an algorithm to 
yield a patient-specific result.  The results derived from the algorithm indicate probability 
of malignancy and are reported as High Level, Moderate Level, or No Significant Level, 
along with an associated percent risk of malignancy. 
o All Nodify CDT testing is performed at Biodesix’s De Soto, Kansas laboratory. 
Nodify CDT is covered by the MAC for Kansas, WPS GHA, and was approved as 
an ADLT on June 30, 2023.  ADLT status requires proof that a clinical diagnostic 
laboratory test is covered by Medicare Part B, demonstrating that Nodify CDT is 
covered.4  
 
 
1 Oncology (lung), mass spectrometric analysis of galectin-3-binding protein and scavenger receptor cysteine-rich 
type 1 protein M130, with five clinical risk factors (age, smoking status, nodule diameter, nodule-spiculation status 
and nodule location), utilizing plasma, algorithm reported as a categorical probability of malignancy.  
2 See Local Coverage Determination (LCD): MolDX: BDX-XL2 (L37216). 
3 Oncology (lung), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) of 7 autoantibodies (p53, NY-ESO-1, CAGE, 
GBU4-5, SOX2, MAGE A4, and HuD), plasma, algorithm reported as a categorical result for risk of malignancy. 
4 42 C.F.R. § 414.502.  
 
 
• VeriStrat: Biodesix’s sole source VeriStrat® test (CPT 81538)5, is used by physicians to 
guide therapy decisions for patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).  
The VeriStrat test is a highly complex test measuring the levels of clinically relevant 
proteins combined by an algorithm into a single clinically validated result.  VeriStrat 
provides patient-specific information to the treating physician to guide therapy decisions 
when deciding between standard of care treatment options, allowing physicians a more 
informed alternative to treating the patient based on population statistics. 
o The MAC for Colorado, Novitas Solutions, Inc., has jurisdiction over the 
coverage and pricing determinations for the VeriStrat test.  VeriStrat is covered 
by Medicare Part B under Novitas’ LCD L35396.6  CMS approved VeriStrat as 
an ADLT on December 21, 2018. 
 
II. 
Responses to RFI Questions 
Below we offer responses to the specific questions raised by the agency in the RFI.  
a. How do prior authorization requirements for laboratory tests and DMEPOS items 
currently impact patient care and health care provider burden?”  
Applicable law and Medicare policy establish clear obligations on the part of MAOs to cover items 
and services consistent with applicable Medicare coverage policies.  Section 1852(a)(1)(A) of the 
Social Security Act establishes the general requirement that “each Medicare+Choice plan shall 
provide to members enrolled under this part…benefits under the original medicare fee-for-service 
program option.”  Under 42 C.F.R. § 422.101(a), MAOs must “[p]rovide coverage of, by 
furnishing, arranging for, or making payment for, all services that are covered by Part A and Part 
B of Medicare.”   
Section 422.101(b)(3) explicitly requires MA organizations to “[c]omply with [w]ritten coverage 
decisions of local Medicare contractors.”  Most relevantly to Biodesix’s tests, chapter 4, section 
90.4.1 of the Medicare Managed Care Manual establishes the policy for a scenario where “one 
Medicare A/B MAC processes all of the claims for a particular Medicare-covered item or service 
for all Medicare beneficiaries around the country.”  In these circumstances, “MA plans must follow 
the coverage policy reflected in an LCD issued by the A/B MAC that enrolled the provider and 
processes all of the Medicare claims for that item or service.” 
Biodesix agrees with the agency’s view that “[p]rior authorization requirements from health 
insurers for laboratory tests…have emerged, in some instances, as a potential barrier to care and 
coverage, impacting both patients and health care providers.”7  While MAOs are not directly barred 
from using prior authorization, the Medicare Managed Care Manual is clear that “[p]lans may not 
 
5 Oncology (lung), mass spectrometric 8-protein signature, including amyloid A, utilizing serum, prognostic and 
predictive algorithm reported as good versus poor overall survival. 
6 See Local Coverage Determination (LCD): Biomarkers for Oncology (L34396). 
7 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, 20014 (Apr. 14, 2026). 
 
 
implement utilization management protocols that create inappropriate barriers to needed care.”8  
In other words, MAOs are not permitted to use prior authorization or other types of utilization 
management to make an end run around their obligations to cover items and services consistent 
with original Medicare.     
Unfortunately, as the agency notes in the RFI, it is all too common for MAOs to use prior 
authorization to do exactly that.  Biodesix recommends that CMS curtail MAOs’ ability to misuse 
prior authorization by barring the use of prior authorization for an item or service covered under 
an NCD or LCD.  Biodesix’s LCD-covered tests are subject to detailed coverage criteria, which 
the MACs have shown they can operationalize without prior authorization.  These coverage criteria 
are implemented by the MACs without prior authorization, and there is no reason why MAOs 
should not be able to do the same.  The Trump Administration has already secured commitments 
from insurers to limit the volume of medical services subject to prior authorization9, and NCD and 
LCD-covered items and services are plainly a category of benefits for which the downsides of 
permitting prior authorization from the perspective of patient access outweigh any benefits of its 
imposition.  
b. What are possible outcomes of more MACs, MA plans, or non-Medicare payers 
allowing a TRF to be valid medical documentation to show that a laboratory test is 
reasonable and necessary? 
Biodesix also wishes to comment on the specific concerns raised by the agency with MAOs’ use 
of prior authorization as currently operationalized.  The RFI states that “when applying prior 
authorization for basic benefits, prior authorization processes for MA coordinated care plans may 
only be used to confirm the presence of diagnoses or other medical criteria that are the basis for 
coverage determinations for the specific item or service or to ensure an item or service is medically 
necessary based on standards specified in 42 CFR 422.101(c)(1).”10  The agency goes on to note 
that in performing prior authorizations, “some MACs and MA plans may not accept a test 
requisition form (TRF) or a physician attestation as valid medical documentation to establish the 
medical necessity of a laboratory test, which can contribute to administrative burden and consume 
valuable time from health care providers that could otherwise be spent with patients.”11   
MAOs’ approach of not considering information on the TRF as medical record documentation is 
not supported by the applicable Medicare regulations and guidance. First, the regulations at 42 
C.F.R.§ 410.32(d)(3))(i) provide that “upon request by CMS, the entity submitting the claim must 
provide the following information: (A) Documentation of the order for the service billed (including 
information sufficient to enable CMS to identify and contact the ordering physician or 
nonphysician practitioner). (B) Documentation showing accurate processing of the order and 
 
8 Medicare Managed Care Manual, chapter 4, § 110.1.1. 
9 HHS, “HHS Secretary Kennedy, CMS Administrator Oz Secure Industry Pledge to Fix Broken Prior Authorization 
System”, Jun. 23, 2025, available at https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/kennedy-oz-cms-secure-healthcare-industry-
pledge-to-fix-prior-authorization-system.html.  
10 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, 20015 (Apr. 14, 2026). 
11 Id. 
 
 
submission of the claim. (C) Diagnostic or other medical information supplied to the laboratory 
by the ordering physician or nonphysician practitioner, including any ICD-9-CM (now ICD-10-
CM) code or narrative description supplied.”  Under subsection (d)(3)(ii), CMS seeks 
documentation from the ordering physician only “[i]f the documentation provided under paragraph 
(d)(3)(i) of this section does not demonstrate that the service is reasonable and necessary.” 
Chapter 3, section 3.2.3.7 of the Medicare Program Integrity Manual provides similar guidance. 
Under this section, “[w]hen the MACs, CERT, RACs, and UPICs send an [additional 
documentation request (ADR)] for a lab service, the following documentation shall be requested 
from the billing lab: The order for the service billed (including sufficient information to allow the 
reviewer to identify and contact the ordering provider); Verification of accurate processing of the 
order and submission of the claim; and Diagnostic or other medical information supplied to the 
lab by the ordering provider, including any diagnosis codes or narratives.”  The contractor is 
required to “deny the claim if a benefit category, statutory exclusion, or coding issue is in question, 
or send an ADR to the ordering provider in order to determine medical necessity.  The contractor 
shall review information from the lab and find it insufficient before the ordering provider is 
contacted.” 
The coverage review process established by § 410.32(d)(3) and chapter 3, section 3.2.3.7 clearly 
contemplates an initial review of documentation of the order, associated diagnostic information, 
and accurate processing of the order – information typically available from the TRF.  This is 
particularly true for TRFs used by Biodesix and other laboratories performing advanced diagnostic 
testing, as we and peer laboratories use detailed, branded TRFs that collect information directly 
responsive to the coverage criteria for our tests.  Only if the information from the laboratory is 
insufficient is additional documentation requested from the ordering physician.  Plainly, this 
process requires the plan to engage in a good faith review of the information obtained from the 
laboratory, rather than dismissing all information included on the TRF as insufficient to 
demonstrate satisfaction of the coverage criteria    
Furthermore, the individual MACs that process claims for Biodesix’s Nodify XL2, Nodify CDT, 
and VeriStrat tests have their own specific policies requiring consideration of information 
contained on the TRF when adjudicating coverage.  For instance, Nodify XL2 and Nodify CDT 
are covered by the local MAC with jurisdiction over the Kansas laboratory at which both tests are 
performed, WPS.  Through the multi-MAC MolDX program in which it participates, WPS has 
established a clear policy that “[t]est requisition forms are part of the medical record.  When 
requisition forms include complete information validating medical necessity, such as qualifying 
clinical information that demonstrate test coverage criteria are met, the requisition form may 
be sufficient to determine if the service is reasonable and necessary without other medical 
information from the ordering provider.”12 
 
12 WPS Insurance Corporation, Article A59798, available at https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-
database/view/article.aspx?articleid=59798&ver=2&bc=0.  
 
 
Similarly, VeriStrat is covered by Novitas Solutions, the MAC with jurisdiction over the Colorado 
laboratory at which the test is performed.  Novitas has established a policy under which “[o]rders 
and test results for the test performed” are among the categories of medical records that may be 
submitted with an initial claim to support coverage.13  Because these documentation policies that 
include the requisition form as part of the medical record are used to determine coverage of Nodify 
XL2, Nodify CDT, and VeriStrat under the LCDs that govern coverage for these tests nationwide, 
MAOs are obligated by chapter 4, section 90.4.1 of the Managed Care Manual to follow these 
policies to determine whether to approve prior authorization for testing. 
It may, in some cases, be appropriate for an MAO to request full medical records in order to 
confirm that the information provided on the TRF is consistent with the patient’s broader clinical 
history.  However, as noted above, the CMS regulations and MAC guidance make clear that 
requests for full medical records cannot be the MAO’s default position.  Moreover, a rule of reason 
must apply when assessing whether the full medical record supports the TRF.  It would not be 
expected for an ordering physician to believe that it is necessary to repeat all of the information on 
the TRF elsewhere in the medical record.  The full medical record should only raise doubts about 
whether the information on the TRF satisfies the coverage criteria if information elsewhere in the 
medical record contradicts information in the TRF that is material to the satisfaction of the 
applicable medical necessity criteria.  
Biodesix thus urges CMS to use the Final Rule to make clear that 1) MAOs must consider medical 
record information provided on the TRF when determining whether NCD, LCD, and other 
coverage criteria have been satisfied; and 2) MAOs must determine that a test is covered if the 
medical record information on the TRF supports satisfaction of the applicable NCD or LCD 
coverage criteria, unless the information elsewhere in the medical record contradicts the 
information on the TRF. 
c. How frequently are prior authorizations denied because the request was submitted 
after the specimen was collected? 
As indicated in the Proposed Rule, another frequent issue encountered by advanced diagnostic 
laboratories with MAOs is their use of the requirements of the Medicare Part B laboratory DOS 
regulations14 in a manner that undermines laboratories’ ability to obtain timely prior authorization 
for covered services.  For instance, MAOs will determine that the DOS is the date of specimen 
collection and deny a prior authorization request that was submitted after the laboratory 
subsequently received the test order.  The MA plan takes the position that the prior authorization 
must be denied because it was requested after the DOS, even though the test was not performed 
prior to the prior authorization being requested.   
As CMS articulates, MAOs’ use of the Part B laboratory DOS rule in this manner is impermissible, 
and it is “wholly inconsistent with 42 CFR 422.138(b) to apply the DOS policy as a basis to deny 
 
13 See Novitas Solutions, “New process for pathology and laboratory codes,” Aug. 16, 2024, available at 
https://www.novitas-solutions.com/webcenter/portal/MedicareJH/pagebyid?contentId=00294519.  
14 See 42 CFR § 414.510. 
 
 
a request for prior authorization of laboratory services that have not yet been performed.”15  In the 
Final Rule, CMS should require that if the date of specimen collection must be used as the DOS 
for billing purposes, a request for prior authorization must be accepted within 30 days after the 
DOS.  We request a clear and expeditious enforcement pathway to implement this policy.  
d. What other issues exist regarding prior authorization processes for laboratory tests 
and DMEPOS items that technology is not currently addressing? 
We wish to raise two additional issues relative to the use of prior authorization and other utilization 
management techniques by MAOs: 
1. Support CMS guidance on impermissibility of restricting laboratories from requesting 
prior authorization.   
As CMS notes in the RFI, MAOs often forbid laboratories like Biodesix from requesting prior 
authorization for the tests that we offer and furnish, instead obligating the ordering provider to 
obtain the prior authorization.  We submit claims to multiple national and regional plans that 
prevent us from requesting prior authorization directly and instead require the ordering physician 
to obtain prior authorization.  This policy leads both to more errors in prior authorization requests 
and to unnecessary demands on physician practice resources because ordering physicians are less 
familiar with requesting prior authorization for unique diagnostics. 
We strongly support the agency’s confirmation in the Proposed Rule that these restrictions are 
inappropriate: “In the MA context, MA plans must allow laboratories to initiate prior 
authorization requests because a laboratory is a ‘‘provider’’ that furnishes, or intends to 
furnish, services to the enrollee.  See 42 CFR 422.566(c)(1)(ii).”16  As above, we request a clear 
enforcement pathway to ensure the effectuation of this policy.  
2. Request prohibition on burdensome prepayment review requirements for NCD and LCD-
covered tests 
Finally, along with prior authorization, we remain concerned about other mechanisms used by 
MAOs to avoid their obligation to pay for NCD- and LCD-covered tests.  For example, between 
2020 – 2024, one national health plan denied 88% of Biodesix’s Medicare covered Nodify XL2, 
Nodify CDT, and VeriStrat claims for Medicare Advantage enrollees due to the implementation 
of a prepayment review, despite Biodesix providing information to demonstrate that the patients 
met the LCD and coverage criteria for the tests and performing multiple claims analyses for the 
plan.  In particular, the imposition of prepayment review included burdensome requests for 
medical documentation well beyond the TRF and test report, as well as inconsistent review of 
these medical records. This prepayment review methodology resulted in delayed claims 
processing, significant administrative burden on both the laboratory and ordering physician 
 
15 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, 20015 (Apr. 14, 2026).  
16 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, 20014 n.399 (Apr. 14, 2026). 
 
 
offices, increased confusion for the patients, and significant loss of revenue in unpaid, LCD-
compliant, medically necessary, Medicare-covered testing.  
As with prior authorization, Biodesix believes that it is inappropriate for MAOs to be using 
prepayment review for NCD and LCD-covered services, which are subject to well-defined 
coverage criteria that are routinely implemented by MACs without any sort of prepayment review.  
We encourage CMS to clarify that this practice is not permissible.  At minimum, CMS should 
clarify that any prepayment review obligation imposed by a MAO for an NCD- or LCD-covered 
service can be satisfied by information on the TRF responsive to the coverage criteria.  
Conclusion 
For the foregoing reasons, Biodesix applauds CMS’s attention to this issue and policy 
clarifications in the RFI.  Biodesix believes that inappropriate use of prior authorization and 
prepayment review by MAOs for NCD- and LCD-covered services warrant CMS prohibiting the 
use of these utilization management tools for NCD- and LCD-covered services.  Alternatively, 
CMS should:  
• Make clear that the TRF is part of the medical record that must be reviewed by the MAO, 
and that information on the TRF that satisfies an NCD or LCD coverage criterion must be 
accepted absent contradictory information elsewhere in the medical record. 
• Clarify that where the MAO applies the date of specimen collection as the date of service, 
prior authorization can be requested up to 30 days after the specimen collection date. 
• Make clear that any prepayment review obligation imposed by a MAO for an NCD- or 
LCD-covered service can be satisfied by information on the TRF responsive to the 
coverage criteria. 
• Establish a clear, accessible, and expedited process to submit complaints for violations of 
an MAO’s responsibility to cover original Medicare-covered testing.   
Thank you for your review of these issues.  Please contact me at robin.cowie@biodesix.com if you 
have any questions.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Robin H. Cowie 
Chief Financial Officer 
Biodesix, Inc.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Biodesix, Inc., signed by Robin H. Cowie, Chief Financial Officer.
- **Stakeholder type:** Healthcare Provider; Technology/Diagnostics Vendor; Other clinical laboratory.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Enrolled Medicare provider of lung cancer diagnostic laboratory tests, including Nodify XL2, Nodify CDT, and VeriStrat; tests are covered under MAC LCDs and/or approved as Advanced Diagnostic Laboratory Tests.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Biodesix responds to CMS's laboratory-test prior authorization RFI and argues that MA organizations misuse prior authorization and prepayment review to undercut coverage for NCD- and LCD-covered laboratory tests. The commenter asks CMS to prohibit PA for NCD/LCD-covered tests or, at minimum, require MAOs to accept test requisition form documentation, allow post-specimen authorization timing, permit laboratories to initiate PA, and create an expedited enforcement pathway.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL/RFI on laboratory tests and DMEPOS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS by analogy to PA timing; TRANSPARENCY/enforcement; REGULATORY-AUTHORITY as applied to MAO obligations.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Social Security Act §1852(a)(1)(A); 42 CFR §422.101(a), §422.101(b)(3), §422.101(c)(1), §422.138(b), §422.566(c)(1)(ii), §410.32(d)(3), §414.510, §414.502; Medicare Managed Care Manual chapter 4 §§90.4.1 and 110.1.1; Medicare Program Integrity Manual chapter 3 §3.2.3.7.
- **Standards referenced:** No FHIR or NCPDP standards are central; comment focuses on Medicare coverage rules, LCDs, NCDs, ADLTs, TRFs, and prior authorization operations.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prohibit PA for NCD/LCD-Covered Laboratory Tests**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** MAOs must cover original Medicare-covered services and should not use PA to create inappropriate barriers to NCD- or LCD-covered services.
- **Specific request:** Bar MAOs from using prior authorization for items or services covered by an NCD or LCD.

**Topic 2: TRF as Valid Medical Documentation**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Medicare rules and MAC policies contemplate initial review of laboratory order, diagnostic information, and order-processing documentation, which is commonly available on detailed TRFs.
- **Specific request:** Clarify that MAOs must consider TRF information and approve coverage when the TRF satisfies NCD/LCD criteria unless contradicted elsewhere in the medical record.

**Topic 3: Date of Service and Post-Specimen Authorization**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** MAOs sometimes deny PA because a specimen was collected before authorization, even though the test was not performed before the PA request.
- **Specific request:** Require acceptance of PA requests within 30 days after the DOS when specimen collection date must be used as DOS.

**Topic 4: Laboratories Must Be Allowed to Request PA**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support/Clarify
- **Rationale:** Laboratories are providers furnishing or intending to furnish services and are better positioned than ordering physicians to complete PA requests for unique diagnostics.
- **Specific request:** Finalize/confirm that MA plans must allow laboratories to initiate PA requests and establish an enforcement pathway.

**Topic 5: Prepayment Review for NCD/LCD-Covered Tests**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Burdensome prepayment review can function like PA and delay or deny payment for medically necessary LCD-covered testing.
- **Specific request:** Prohibit broad prepayment review for NCD/LCD-covered tests or clarify that TRF information responsive to coverage criteria satisfies prepayment review obligations.

**Topic 6: Enforcement Pathway**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; REGULATORY-AUTHORITY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Clarifications will not be effective without a practical route to report and correct MAO violations.
- **Specific request:** Establish a clear, accessible, expedited complaint and enforcement pathway.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S66-S82:** Responds to the RFI on laboratory tests, especially questions about laboratory PA impact, TRF validity, specimen timing, and technology gaps.
- **Laboratory PA impact RFI:** States that MAO PA can block access to Medicare-covered diagnostic tests and should be prohibited for NCD/LCD-covered services.
- **TRF RFI:** Argues TRFs should be accepted as part of the medical record when they contain coverage-criteria information.
- **Specimen collection timing RFI:** Requests a rule allowing PA submission up to 30 days after specimen collection where the DOS policy applies.
- **Other issues RFI:** Requests confirmation that laboratories may request PA directly and that MAOs may not use prepayment review to evade coverage obligations.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Prohibit MAO prior authorization for NCD- or LCD-covered tests.
2. Clarify MAOs must consider TRF information as medical record documentation.
3. Require coverage where TRF information satisfies NCD/LCD criteria absent contradictory medical record evidence.
4. Allow PA requests up to 30 days after specimen collection when specimen collection is treated as the DOS.
5. Confirm laboratories may initiate PA requests for tests they furnish.
6. Prohibit or restrict prepayment review for NCD/LCD-covered tests.
7. Establish an accessible, expedited enforcement pathway for complaints.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** MAO misuse of PA, refusal to accept TRF documentation, improper DOS-based denials, restrictions on lab-initiated PA, and burdensome prepayment review.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed testing, administrative burden on laboratories and ordering physicians, patient confusion, unpaid medically necessary tests, and reduced access to lung cancer diagnostics.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** MAO policies inconsistent with MAC coverage and documentation practices; plan refusal to operationalize original Medicare coverage rules.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** One national health plan denied 88% of Biodesix's Medicare-covered Nodify XL2, Nodify CDT, and VeriStrat claims for MA enrollees between 2020 and 2024 due to prepayment review.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not primarily research-based; relies on Medicare regulations, manuals, MAC LCDs/articles, ADLT status, and operational experience.
- **Examples provided:** Nodify XL2, Nodify CDT, and VeriStrat tests; WPS and Novitas MAC policies; MAO denial of PA after specimen collection.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Medicare Advantage enrollees needing lung cancer diagnostics, ordering physicians, clinical laboratories, MAOs, MACs, and CMS oversight staff.
- **Economic implications:** Inappropriate denials and prepayment review can cause revenue loss for laboratories and add administrative costs for providers.
- **Technical feasibility:** Issue is less about new technology than policy alignment, documentation acceptance, and enforcement.
- **Patient care impact:** Positive if CMS acts; reducing PA misuse would improve timely access to covered diagnostic testing.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned and modification-focused.
- **Tone:** Technical, legal, and assertive.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The most straightforward way for CMS to address these issues...is to prohibit the use of prior authorization by MAOs for a test covered by an NCD or LCD." - Context: Principal recommendation.
2. "Test requisition forms are part of the medical record." - Context: Citing MAC policy supporting TRF acceptance.
3. "MA plans must allow laboratories to initiate prior authorization requests" - Context: Supporting CMS's proposed clarification.
4. "Between 2020 – 2024, one national health plan denied 88%" - Context: Evidence of harm from prepayment review.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Emphasizes burdens on ordering physicians and laboratories.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Focuses on access to covered lung cancer diagnostics.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Relies heavily on Medicare Advantage statutory/regulatory obligations and manuals.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests clear documentation and enforcement expectations.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Explains real-world lab order, TRF, DOS, and claim workflows.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Indicates technology alone does not solve MAO policy misuse.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requires alignment among MAOs, laboratories, ordering physicians, MACs, and CMS.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Notes unpaid claims, revenue loss, and administrative resource burden.
